analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act rule requiring large employers to offer health coverage or pay a penalty.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the employer health insurance mandate never left the House Ways and Means Committee, dying there with 34 Republican cosponsors and no committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the Affordable Care Act's employer mandate from the tax code — the rule that employers with 50 or more full-time workers must offer affordable health coverage or pay a penalty, along with the paperwork showing they did. It would have taken effect going back to 2014. Large employers would no longer owe penalties or file the reports; workers would lose the legal push that keeps employer coverage in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with 50 or more full-time employees who would otherwise owe the ACA penalty — about $2,000 per uncovered full-time worker — or spend money proving they offer compliant coverage. This falls hardest on industries with many large, low-wage employers, like retail, restaurants, and staffing firms.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes section 4980H of the tax code, the provision requiring employers with 50 or more full-time workers to provide health coverage or pay a penalty, along with the related section 6056 reporting requirement [S3].
Makes the repeal retroactive to periods beginning after December 31, 2013, wiping out penalties for the mandate's first years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers covered through their jobs: the employer penalty is what gives large firms a reason to offer coverage, so removing it opens the door for some employers to drop coverage or shift costs onto employees. The federal government would also lose the penalty revenue.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate is the mechanism that requires large employers to offer affordable coverage; striking it removes the only penalty for dropping that coverage, so some workers could lose their insurance or be asked to pay more of the premium themselves [S2][S3].

The repeal would also eliminate the section 6056 reporting that documents which employers actually offer coverage, taking away the paper trail that tells workers and the IRS whether an employer is meeting its obligation [S3].
Making the repeal retroactive to 2014 would erase penalties already accrued, reducing federal revenue with no offset [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to employers: less paperwork and no penalty exposure, savings that are real but modest per worker and would show up as employer profit, not necessarily as better pay or jobs. The risk falls on workers — if an employer decides the coverage is no longer worth offering, nothing in this bill replaces it. The bill's name promises job protection, but the text is solely a tax-code repeal with no job-creating mechanism in it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Boustany introduced the bill on January 9, 2015, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
Thirty-four Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill received no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the employer coverage requirement stayed on the books, which was the outcome workers on employer health plans and the insurers selling them group coverage were better off with. Large employers hoping to shed the penalty and reporting costs gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Charles Boustany
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: 34 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal of the employer mandate.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where the parties would have been recorded.

industries.industry: Large employers (50+ full-time workers, especially retail, restaurants, and staffing firms)
industries.note: The bill would erase their penalty for not covering workers and the reporting requirement proving compliance, a direct cost saving. The offsetting risk — some employers dropping or thinning coverage — lands on their employees, not on them.

industries.industry: Health insurers selling employer group plans
industries.note: The employer mandate pushes large firms to buy group coverage; repealing it removes that push, shrinking a market insurers depend on. Their interest here runs alongside workers who get coverage through a job.
